summary: NISAR has delivered calibrated L-band radar data only since 17 June 2026. The best radar change detectors compare each pixel with years of its own past; without that, a plain before/after difference mistakes rain and seasonal shifts for change. Cold Start uses the rest of the scene instead. It learns how much change to expect for each kind of land on the same two dates and flags cells that changed more, at a false-alarm rate set in advance. We wrote our hypotheses down before scoring and tested them on two 2026 Oregon fires: McCully, then Austin, chosen by rules written down beforehand. The false-alarm setting held on all 24 held-out checks. On both fires, the model flagged far less land outside the mapped perimeter than the standard before/after method (8.5% vs 23.6%, and 27.8% vs 53.4%). Its lead over a simpler land-type baseline did not hold up in Austin, where the two tied. A public app shows the maps, each cell's radar history and a ranked list of places to check. A flag shows radar change; someone still has to confirm damage. NISAR images Earth's land every 12 days, so its change maps shouldn't have to wait years for an archive.
details:
What it does

Cold Start maps surface change between two NISAR acquisitions at 100 m resolution, at a false-alarm rate the user picks, and shows the result in a web app. The main case is the 2026 McCully Fire in Oregon, comparing 18 August with 23 September. The app also includes a second fire, Austin (27 July to 7 October), which we scored as a pre-registered replication.

How it works

1. For each fire, it reads eleven NISAR L2 GCOV scenes from one orbit track through the Alaska Satellite Facility. It streams only the area around the fire, about 0.4 GB per scene instead of 7.5 GB.

2. HH and HV backscatter are averaged to 100 m cells and converted to decibels. Water, steep terrain, and missing cells are masked out.

3. For a pair of dates, a gradient-boosted quantile regression predicts each cell's expected change and its 5% to 95% range from the cell's earlier backscatter, polarization ratio, texture, terrain factor, and land class. The model is cross-fitted over 10 km tiles, so no cell is scored by a model that saw its own neighbourhood.

4. A cell's score is how far its observed change falls from the predicted value, measured in units of the predicted spread.

5. The alarm threshold comes from conformal calibration on date pairs with no fire, so the false-alarm rate is fixed before the event is examined.

6. Three baselines run on the same grid: the standard log-ratio, a per-pixel z-score on a short history, and change minus the land-class median.

How we tested it

Before scoring the fire, we committed two hypotheses and every setting to the repository, and we used the fire perimeter only for evaluation. H1 says that at 50% recall our model flags less land outside the perimeter than every baseline, with 95% bootstrap intervals that exclude zero. H3 says the calibrated threshold delivers its stated rate on date pairs it never saw. On McCully, both passed: the model flagged 8.5% of outside land, against 12.8% for the best baseline and 23.6% for the standard log-ratio.

Replication

We then picked a second fire, the Austin Fire in Oregon, using rules we committed to before processing any of its data, and ran the same frozen pipeline and settings. H3 passed again (10 of 10 held-out checks, so 24 of 24 across both fires). H1 failed. The model beat the log-ratio and the short-history z-score again but tied the land-type baseline, flagging 27.8% of outside land at 50% recall against the baseline's 27.9%. The pre-registration and this result are both in the repository and in the app.

Exploratory check, added after the main results (post hoc)

Agencies mapped other fires in both study windows in 2026. We had left their cells out of every score, so afterwards we looked at how often each method flagged them. Our model flagged cells inside those fires 10.4 times (McCully) and 24 times (Austin) as often as ordinary land. The land-type baseline managed 9.6 and 10.8 times, and the standard log-ratio 3.0 and 0.4 times. The land-type baseline flags almost as large a share of those fires as we do (25% and 30%, against our 27% and 36%); our higher Austin multiplier comes mostly from flagging less ordinary land (1.5% against 2.8%). On Austin, the model's three largest places to check lie inside the Grasshopper Fire, which was never used as a label. Still, a flag inside a mapped perimeter does not by itself confirm fire damage or detection, since perimeters are outlines and we don't know when each cell burned. We chose this check after seeing the results, so it is not a test.

What we found about the radar

Both polarizations matter. With HH or HV alone, false alarms rose from 8.5% to about 14.5%. Shifts of half a decibel to a decibel across the whole scene between passes are routine, and a plain before/after difference flags them as change.

Benefits and intended impact

We built it as a triage aid rather than an operational system. After an event, an analyst chooses how many false alarms they can accept and sees where the radar changed more than similar land did. They can open any place's radar history and work down a ranked list of places, setting aside fires that are already mapped so that unexplained change comes up first. Flags still need checking against other imagery or on the ground before anyone calls them damage. The main benefit is getting change maps from a new sensor without waiting years for a baseline, with a false-alarm rate that is stated up front and then checked, in an app that shows its own evidence and limits. Before real use, it would need more events and sites, comparison with optical burn-severity maps, and field checks. We'd like it to help make NISAR useful for disturbance alerts in its first year, and to show one way of testing a method like this honestly.

What's new about it

Pixel-history methods need years of data for every pixel. We borrow context from thousands of similar cells on the same two dates instead, and conformal calibration lets us state the false-alarm rate in advance. We also tested it like a study, with hypotheses committed before scoring and a pre-registered replication, and we report the hypothesis that failed alongside the one that passed.

Things we weighed

Every false alarm costs an analyst time, so we set and checked the false-alarm rate instead of assuming it. Full scenes are large, so the pipeline streams only the area it needs. We wanted the app to work for people who aren't radar specialists, so it is written in plain language. We also tried to be clear about the limits. Two fires are a small sample, and on the second the model only tied the land-type baseline. Both burns gave a modest signal: at the default setting the model flags 38% (McCully) and 12% (Austin) of the cells inside the perimeter, and most of its flags lie outside it. Perimeters are outlines rather than cell-by-cell burn maps, so flags outside them count as false alarms without being confirmed errors. Most of the calibration stability comes from normalizing by land type, which a simple baseline also does. We did not test rainfall as an input.

Tools

The pipeline is Python 3.11 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, h5py, rasterio, shapely, pyproj, matplotlib, PyYAML, and asf_search. The app uses Streamlit, Folium, and streamlit-folium and is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. The 45 tests run under pytest; the code lives in Git and GitHub, and we built the slides with PptxGenJS. We didn't need special hardware and everything ran on an ordinary Windows PC, streaming data over the internet.
